# Higher chromatic Thom spectra via unstable homotopy theory

**Authors:** S. K. Devalapurkar Email address: sdevalapurkar@math.harvard.edu

## Abstract

We investigate implications of an old conjecture in unstable homotopy theory related to the Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer theorem and a conjecture about the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -topological Hochschild cohomology of certain Thom spectra (denoted $A$ , $B$ , and $T(n)$ ) related to Ravenel’s $X(p^{n})$ . We show that these conjectures imply that the orientations $\mathrm{MSpin}\to\mathrm{bo}$ and $\mathrm{MString}\to\mathrm{tmf}$ admit spectrum-level splittings. This is shown by generalizing a theorem of Hopkins and Mahowald, which constructs $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ as a Thom spectrum, to construct $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ , $\mathrm{bo}$ , and $\mathrm{tmf}$ as Thom spectra (albeit over $T(n)$ , $A$ , and $B$ respectively, and not over the sphere). This interpretation of $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ , $\mathrm{bo}$ , and $\mathrm{tmf}$ offers a new perspective on Wood equivalences of the form $\mathrm{bo}\wedge C\eta\simeq\mathrm{bu}$ : they are related to the existence of certain EHP sequences in unstable homotopy theory. This construction of $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ also provides a different lens on the nilpotence theorem. Finally, we prove a $C_{2}$ -equivariant analogue of our construction, describing $\underline{\mathrm{H}\mathbf{Z}}$ as a Thom spectrum.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Statement of the main results

One of the goals of this article is to describe a program to prove the following old conjecture (studied, for instance, in [Lau04, LS19], and discussed informally in many places, such as [MR09, Section 7]):

#### Conjecture 1.1.1.

The Ando-Hopkins-Rezk orientation (see [AHR10]) $\mathrm{MString}\to\mathrm{tmf}$ admits a spectrum-level splitting.

The key idea in our program is to provide a universal property for mapping out of the spectrum $\mathrm{tmf}$ . We give a proof which is conditional on an old conjecture from unstable homotopy theory stemming from the Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer theorem and a conjecture about the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -topological Hochschild cohomology of certain Thom spectra (the latter of which simplifies the proof of the nilpotence theorem from [DHS88]). This universal property exhibits $\mathrm{tmf}$ as a certain Thom spectrum, similarly to the Hopkins-Mahowald construction of $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ and $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ as Thom spectra.

To illustrate the gist of our argument in a simpler case, recall Thom’s classical result from [Tho54]: the unoriented cobordism spectrum $\mathrm{MO}$ is a wedge of suspensions of $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{2}$ . The simplest way to do so is to show that $\mathrm{MO}$ is an $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{2}$ -module, which in turn can be done by constructing an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -map $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{2}\to\mathrm{MO}$ . The construction of such a map is supplied by the following theorem of Hopkins and Mahowald:

#### Theorem (Hopkins-Mahowald; see [Mah79] and [MRS01, Lemma 3.3]).

Let $\mu:\Omega^{2}S^{3}\to\mathrm{BO}$ denote the real vector bundle over $\Omega^{2}S^{3}$ induced by extending the map $S^{1}\to\mathrm{BO}$ classifying the Möbius bundle. Then the Thom spectrum of $\mu$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{2}$ as an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -algebra.

#### Remark 1.1.2.

The Thomification of the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -map $\mu:\Omega^{2}S^{3}\to\mathrm{BO}$ produces the desired $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -splitting $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{2}\to\mathrm{MO}$ .

Our argument for Conjecture 1.1.1 takes this approach: we shall show that an old conjecture from unstable homotopy theory and a conjecture about the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -topological Hochschild cohomology of certain Thom spectra provide a construction of $\mathrm{tmf}$ (as well as $\mathrm{bo}$ and $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle$ ) as a Thom spectrum, and utilize the resulting universal property of $\mathrm{tmf}$ to construct an (unstructured) map $\mathrm{tmf}\to\mathrm{MString}$ .

Mahowald was the first to consider the question of constructing spectra like $\mathrm{bo}$ and $\mathrm{tmf}$ as Thom spectra (see [Mah87]). Later work by Rudyak in [Rud98] sharpened Mahowald’s results to show that $\mathrm{bo}$ and $\mathrm{bu}$ cannot appear as the Thom spectrum of a $p$ -complete spherical fibration. In [AHL09], Angeltveit-Hill-Lawson gave an alternative proof of this fact under the assumption that the $p$ -complete spherical fibration is classified by a map of $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -spaces. Recently, Chatham has shown in [Cha19] that $\mathrm{tmf}^{\wedge}_{2}$ cannot appear as the Thom spectrum of a structured $2$ -complete spherical fibration over a loop space. Our goal is to argue that these issues are alleviated if we replace “spherical fibrations” with “bundles of $R$ -lines” for certain well-behaved spectra $R$ .

The first hint of $\mathrm{tmf}$ being a generalized Thom spectrum comes from a conjecture of Hopkins and Hahn regarding a construction of the truncated Brown-Peterson spectra $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle$ as Thom spectra. To state this conjecture, we need to recall some definitions. Recall (see [DHS88]) that $X(n)$ denotes the Thom spectrum of the map $\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)\to\Omega\mathrm{SU}\simeq\mathrm{BU}$ . Upon completion at a prime $p$ , the spectra $X(k)$ for $p^{n}\leq k\leq p^{n+1}-1$ split as a direct sum of suspensions of certain homotopy commutative ring spectra $T(n)$ , which in turn filter the gap between the $p$ -complete sphere spectrum and $\mathrm{BP}$ (in the sense that $T(0)=\mathbb{S}$ and $T(\infty)=\mathrm{BP}$ ). Then:

#### Conjecture 1.1.3 (Hahn, Hopkins; unpublished).

There is a map $f:\Omega^{2}S^{|v_{n}|+3}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(T(n))$ , which detects an indecomposable element $v_{n}\in\pi_{|v_{n}|}T(n)$ on the bottom cell of the source, whose Thom spectrum is a form of $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ .

The primary obstruction to proving that a map $f$ as in Conjecture 1.1.3 exists stems from the failure of $T(n)$ to be an $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -ring (due to Lawson; [Law20, Example 1.5.31]). If $R$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ - or $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring spectrum, let $\mathfrak{Z}_{3}(R)$ denote the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -topological Hochschild cohomology of $R$ (see Definition 3.3.2). Hahn suggested that one way to get past the failure of $T(n)$ to be an $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -ring would be via the following conjecture:

#### Conjecture 1.1.4 (Hahn).

There is an indecomposable element $v_{n}\in\pi_{|v_{n}|}T(n)$ which lifts to the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -topological Hochschild cohomology $\mathfrak{Z}_{3}(X(p^{n}))$ of $X(p^{n})$ .

We do not know how to prove this conjecture (and have no opinion on whether or not it is true). We shall instead show that Conjecture 1.1.3 is implied by the two conjectures alluded to above. We shall momentarily state these conjectures precisely as Conjectures D and E; let us first state our main results.

We need to introduce some notation. Let $y(n)$ (resp. $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ ) denote the Mahowald-Ravenel-Shick spectrum, constructed as a Thom spectrum over $\Omega J_{p^{n}-1}(S^{2})$ (resp. $\Omega J_{p^{n}-1}(S^{2})\langle 2\rangle$ ) introduced in [MRS01] to study the telescope conjecture (resp. in [AQ19] as $z(n)$ ). Let $A$ denote the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -quotient $\mathbb{S}/\!\!/\nu$ of the sphere spectrum by $\nu\in\pi_{3}(\mathbb{S})$ ; its mod $2$ homology is $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(A)\cong\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1}^{4}]$ . The spectrum $A$ has been intensely studied by Mahowald and his coauthors in (for instance) [Mah79, DM81, Mah81b, Mah81a, Mah82, MU77], where it is often denoted $X_{5}$ . (See Remark 2.1.8 for motivation for the term “ $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -quotient”.) Let $B$ denote the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring introduced in [Dev19b, Construction 3.1]; it has been briefly studied under the name $\overline{X}$ in [HM02]. It may be constructed as the Thom spectrum of a vector bundle over an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -space $N$ which sits in a fiber sequence $\Omega S^{9}\to N\to\Omega S^{13}$ . The mod $2$ homology of $B$ is $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(B)\cong\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1}^{8},\zeta_{2}^{4}]$ .

We also need to recall some unstable homotopy theory. In [CMN79a, CMN79b, Nei81], Cohen, Moore, and Neisendorfer constructed a map $\phi_{n}:\Omega^{2}S^{2n+1}\to S^{2n-1}$ whose composite with the double suspension $E^{2}:S^{2n-1}\to\Omega^{2}S^{2n+1}$ is the degree $p$ map. (The symbol $E$ stands for “Einhängung”, which is German for “suspension”.) Such a map was also constructed by Gray in [Gra89b, Gra88]. In Section 4.1, we introduce the related notion of a charming map (Definition 4.1.1), one example of which is the Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer map.

Our main result is then:

#### Theorem A.

Suppose $R$ is a base spectrum of height $n$ as in the second line of Table 1. Let $K_{n+1}$ denote the fiber of a charming map $\Omega^{2}S^{2p^{n+1}+1}\to S^{2p^{n+1}-1}$ . Then Conjectures D and E imply that there is a map $\mu:K_{n+1}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)$ such that the mod $p$ homology of the Thom spectrum $K_{n+1}^{\mu}$ is isomorphic to the mod $p$ homology of the associated designer chromatic spectrum ${\Theta}(R)$ as a Steenrod comodule11 1 We elected to use the symbol ${\Theta}$ because the first two letters of the English spelling of ${\Theta}$ and of Thom’s name agree..

If $R$ is any base spectrum other than $B$ , the Thom spectrum $K_{n+1}^{\mu}$ is equivalent to ${\Theta}(R)$ upon $p$ -completion for every prime $p$ . If Conjecture F is true, then the same is true for $B$ : the Thom spectrum $K_{n+1}^{\mu}$ is equivalent to ${\Theta}(B)=\mathrm{tmf}$ upon $2$ -completion.

| Height | 0 | 1 | 2 | $n$ | $n$ | $n$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base spectrum $R$ | $\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p}$ | $A$ | $B$ | $T(n)$ | $y(n)$ | $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ |
| Designer chromatic spectrum ${\Theta}(R)$ | $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ | $\mathrm{bo}$ | $\mathrm{tmf}$ | $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle$ | $k(n)$ | $k_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ |

*Table 1. To go from a base spectrum “of height $n$ ”, say $R$ , in the second line to the third, one takes the Thom spectrum of a bundle of $R$ -lines over $K_{n+1}$ .*

Making sense of Theorem A relies on knowing that $T(n)$ admits the structure of an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring; this is proved in [BL21]; see also Warning 3.1.6. Note that the spectra $A$ , $B$ , $y(n)$ , and $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ all admit $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -structures by construction. In Remark 5.4.7, we sketch how Theorem A relates to the proof of the nilpotence theorem.

Although the form of Theorem A does not resemble Conjecture 1.1.3, we show that Theorem A implies the following result.

#### Corollary B.

Conjectures D and E imply Conjecture 1.1.3.

In the case $n=0$ , Corollary B recovers the Hopkins-Mahowald theorem constructing $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ . Moreover, Corollary B is true unconditionally when $n=0,1$ .

Using the resulting universal property of $\mathrm{tmf}$ , we obtain a result pertaining to Conjecture 1.1.1.

#### Theorem C.

Assume that the composite $\mathfrak{Z}_{3}(B)\to B\to\mathrm{MString}$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -map. Then Conjectures D, E, and F imply that there is a spectrum-level unital splitting of the Ando-Hopkins-Rezk orientation $\mathrm{MString}_{(2)}\to\mathrm{tmf}_{(2)}$ .

In particular, Conjecture 1.1.1 follows (at least after localizing at $p=2$ ; a slight modification of our arguments should work at any prime). We believe that the assumption that the composite $\mathfrak{Z}_{3}(B)\to B\to\mathrm{MString}$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -map is too strong: we believe that it can be removed using special properties of fibers of charming maps, and we will return to this in future work.

We stress that these splittings are unstructured; it seems unlikely that they can be refined to structured splittings. In [Dev19b], we showed (unconditionally) that the Ando-Hopkins-Rezk orientation $\mathrm{MString}\to\mathrm{tmf}$ induces a surjection on homotopy, a result which is clearly implied by Theorem C.

We remark that the argument used to prove Theorem C shows that if the composite $\mathfrak{Z}_{3}(A)\to A\to\mathrm{MSpin}$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -map, then Conjectures D and E imply that there is a spectrum-level unital splitting of the Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro orientation $\mathrm{MSpin}\to\mathrm{bo}$ . This splitting was originally proved unconditionally (i.e., without assuming Conjecture D or Conjecture E) by Anderson-Brown-Peterson in [ABP67] via a calculation with the Adams spectral sequence.

### 1.2. The statements of Conjectures D, E, and F

We first state Conjecture D. The second part of this conjecture is a compilation of several old conjectures in unstable homotopy theory originally made by Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer, Gray, and Selick in [CMN79a, CMN79b, Nei81, Gra89b, Gra88, Sel77]. The statement we shall give momentarily differs slightly from the statements made in the literature: for instance, in Conjecture D(b), we demand a $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -space splitting (Notation 2.2.6), rather than merely an H-space splitting.

#### Conjecture D.

The following statements are true:

- (a) The homotopy fiber of any charming map (Definition 4.1.1) is equivalent as a loop space to the loop space on an Anick space (Definition 4.1.3).

- (b) There exists a $p$ -local charming map $f:\Omega^{2}S^{2p^{n}+1}\to S^{2p^{n}-1}$ whose homotopy fiber admits a $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -space retraction off of $\Omega^{2}(S^{2p^{n}}/p)$ . There are also integrally defined maps $\Omega^{2}S^{9}\to S^{7}$ and $\Omega^{2}S^{17}\to S^{15}$ whose composites with the double suspension on $S^{7}$ and $S^{15}$ respectively are the degree $2$ maps. Moreover, their homotopy fibers $K_{2}$ and $K_{3}$ (respectively) admit deloopings, and admit $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -space retractions off $\Omega^{2}(S^{8}/2)$ and $\Omega^{2}(S^{16}/2)$ (respectively).

Next, we turn to Conjecture E. This conjecture is concerned with the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -topological Hochschild cohomology of the Thom spectra $X(p^{n}-1)_{(p)}$ , $A$ , and $B$ introduced above.

#### Conjecture E.

Let $n\geq 0$ be an integer. Let $R$ denote $X(p^{n+1}-1)_{(p)}$ , $A$ (in which case $n=1$ ), or $B$ (in which case $n=2$ ). Then the element $\sigma_{n}\in\pi_{|v_{n}|-1}R$ lifts to the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -topological Hochschild cohomology $\mathfrak{Z}_{3}(R)$ of $R$ , and is $p$ -torsion in $\pi_{\ast}\mathfrak{Z}_{3}(R)$ if $R=X(p^{n+1}-1)_{(p)}$ , and is $2$ -torsion in $\pi_{\ast}\mathfrak{Z}_{3}(R)$ if $R=A$ or $B$ .

Finally, we state Conjecture F. It is inspired by [AP76, AL17]. We believe this conjecture is the most approachable of the conjectures stated here.

#### Conjecture F.

Suppose $X$ is a spectrum which is bounded below and whose homotopy groups are finitely generated over $\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ . If there is an isomorphism $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(X;\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{tmf};\mathbf{F}_{p})$ of Steenrod comodules, then there is a homotopy equivalence $X^{\wedge}_{p}\to\mathrm{tmf}^{\wedge}_{p}$ of spectra.

After proving Theorem A and Theorem C, we explore relationships between the different spectra appearing on the second line of Table 1 in the remainder of the article. In particular, we prove analogues of Wood’s equivalence $\mathrm{bo}\wedge C\eta\simeq\mathrm{bu}$ (see also [Mat16]) for these spectra. We argue that these are related to the existence of certain EHP sequences.

Finally, we describe a $C_{2}$ -equivariant analogue of Corollary B at $n=1$ as Theorem 7.2.1, independently of a $C_{2}$ -equivariant analogue of Conjecture D and Conjecture E. This result constructs $\mathrm{H}\underline{\mathbf{Z}}$ as a Thom spectrum of an equivariant bundle of invertible $T(1)_{\mathbf{R}}$ -modules over $\Omega^{\rho}S^{2\rho+1}$ , where $T(1)_{\mathbf{R}}$ is the free $\mathbf{E}_{{\sigma}}$ -algebra with a nullhomotopy of the equivariant Hopf map $\widetilde{\eta}\in\pi_{\sigma}(\mathbb{S})$ , and $\rho$ and $\sigma$ are the regular and sign representations of $C_{2}$ , respectively. This uses results of Behrens-Wilson and Hahn-Wilson from [BW18, HW20]. We believe there is a similar result at odd primes, but we defer discussion of this. We discuss why our methods do not work to yield $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle_{\mathbf{R}}$ for $n\geq 1$ as in Corollary B.

### 1.3. Outline

Section 2 contains a review some of the theory of Thom spectra from the modern perspective, as well as the proof of the classical Hopkins-Mahowald theorem. The content reviewed in this section will appear in various guises throughout this project, hence its inclusion.

In Section 3, we study certain $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -rings; most of them appear as Thom spectra over the sphere. For instance, we recall some facts about Ravenel’s $X(n)$ spectra, and then define and prove properties about the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -rings $A$ and $B$ used in the statement of Theorem A. We state Conjecture E, and discuss (Remark 5.4.7) its relation to the nilpotence theorem, in this section.

In Section 4, we recall some unstable homotopy theory, such as the Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer map and the fiber of the double suspension. These concepts do not show up often in stable homotopy theory, so we hope this section provides useful background to the reader. We state Conjecture D, and then explore properties of Thom spectra of bundles defined over Anick spaces.

In Section 5, we state and prove Theorem A and Corollary B, and state several easy consequences of Theorem A.

In Section 6, we study some applications of Theorem A. For instance, we use it to prove Theorem C, which is concerned with the splitting of certain cobordism spectra. In a previous version of this article, we had two subsections discussing Wood-like equivalences, and topological Hochschild homology of the chromatic Thom spectra of Table 1. However, while making revisions to this article, we decided to split these two sections off into separate articles [Dev22a, Dev22b].

In Section 7, we prove an equivariant analogue of Corollary B at height $1$ . We construct equivariant analogues of $X(n)$ and $A$ , and describe why our methods fail to produce an equivariant analogue of Corollary B at all heights, even granting an analogue of Conjecture D and Conjecture E.

Finally, in Section 8, we suggest some directions for future research. There are also numerous interesting questions arising from our work, which we have indicated in the body of the article.

### Conventions

Unless indicated otherwise, or if it goes against conventional notational choices, a Latin letter with a numerical subscript (such as $x_{5}$ ) denotes an element of degree given by its subscript. If $X$ is a space and $R$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring spectrum, then $X^{\mu}$ will denote the Thom spectrum of some bundle of invertible $R$ -modules determined by a map $\mu:X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)$ . We shall often quietly localize or complete at an implicit prime $p$ . Although we have tried to be careful, all limits and colimits will be homotopy limits and colimits; we apologize for any inconvenience this might cause.

We shall denote by $P^{k}(p)$ the mod $p$ Moore space $S^{k-1}\cup_{p}e^{k}$ with top cell in dimension $k$ . The symbols $\zeta_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}$ will denote the conjugates of the Milnor generators (commonly written nowadays as $\xi_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}$ , although, as Haynes Miller pointed out to me, our notation for the conjugates was Milnor’s original notation) in degrees $2(p^{i}-1)$ and $2p^{i}-1$ for $p>2$ and $2^{i}-1$ (for $\zeta_{i}$ ) at $p=2$ . Unfortunately, we will use $A$ to denote the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring in appearing in Table 1, and write $A_{\ast}$ to denote the dual Steenrod algebra. We hope this does not cause any confusion, since we will always denote the homotopy groups of $A$ by $\pi_{\ast}A$ and not $A_{\ast}$ .

If $\mathcal{O}$ is an operad, we will simply write $\mathcal{O}$ -ring to denote an $\mathcal{O}$ -algebra object in spectra. A map of $\mathcal{O}$ -rings respecting the $\mathcal{O}$ -algebra structure will often simply be called a $\mathcal{O}$ -map. Unless it is clear that we mean otherwise, all modules over non- ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -algebras will be left modules.

Hood Chatham pointed out to me that $S^{3}\langle 4\rangle$ would be the correct notation for what we denote by $S^{3}\langle 3\rangle=\fib(S^{3}\to K(\mathbf{Z},3))$ . Unfortunately, the literature seems to have chosen $S^{3}\langle 3\rangle$ as the preferred notation, so we stick to that in this project.

When we write that Theorem A, Corollary B, or Theorem C implies a statement P, we mean that Conjectures D and Conjecture E (and Conjecture F, if the intended application is to $\mathrm{tmf}$ ) imply P via Theorem A, Corollary B, or Theorem C.

## 2. Background, and some classical positive and negative results

### 2.1. Background on Thom spectra

In this section, we will recall some facts about Thom spectra and their universal properties; the discussion is motivated by [ABG+14].

#### Definition 2.1.1.

Let $A$ be an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring, and let $\mu:X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)$ be a map of spaces. The Thom $A$ -module $X^{\mu}$ is defined as the homotopy pushout

$$ \textstyle{\Sigma^{\infty}_{+}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Sigma^{\infty}_{+}\fib(\mu)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{X^{\mu}.} $$

#### Remark 2.1.2.

Let $A$ be an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring, and let $\mu:X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)$ be a map of spaces. The Thom $A$ -module $X^{\mu}$ is the homotopy colimit of the functor $X\xrightarrow{\mu}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)\to\mathrm{Mod}(A)$ , where we have abused notation by identifying $X$ with its associated Kan complex. If $A$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ - $R$ -algebra, then the $R$ -module underlying $X$ can be identified with the homotopy colimit of the composite functor

$$ X\xrightarrow{\mu}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)\to\mathrm{B}\Aut_{R}(A)\to\mathrm{Mod}(R), $$

where we have identified $X$ with its associated Kan complex. The space $\mathrm{B}\Aut_{R}(A)$ can be regarded as the maximal subgroupoid of $\mathrm{Mod}(R)$ spanned by the object $A$ .

The following is immediate from the description of the Thom spectrum as a Kan extension:

#### Proposition 2.1.3.

Let $R$ and $R^{\prime}$ be $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -rings with an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring map $R\to R^{\prime}$ exhibiting $R^{\prime}$ as a right $R$ -module. If $f:X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)$ is a map of spaces, then the Thom spectrum of the composite $X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R^{\prime})$ is the base-change $X^{f}\wedge_{R}R^{\prime}$ of the (left) $R$ -module Thom spectrum $X^{f}$ .

#### Corollary 2.1.4.

Let $R$ and $R^{\prime}$ be $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -rings with an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring map $R\to R^{\prime}$ exhibiting $R^{\prime}$ as a right $R$ -module. If $f:X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)$ is a map of spaces such that the the composite $X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R^{\prime})$ is null, then there is an equivalence $X^{f}\wedge_{R}R^{\prime}\simeq R^{\prime}\wedge\Sigma^{\infty}_{+}X$ .

Moreover (see e.g. [AB19, Corollary 3.2]):

#### Proposition 2.1.5.

Let $X$ be a $k$ -fold loop space, and let $R$ be an $\mathbf{E}_{{k+1}}$ -ring. Then the Thom spectrum of an $\mathbf{E}_{{k}}$ -map $X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{k}}$ - $R$ -algebra.

We will repeatedly use the following classical result, which is again a consequence of the observation that Thom spectra are colimits, as well as the fact that total spaces of fibrations may be expressed as colimits; see also [Bea17, Theorem 1].

#### Proposition 2.1.6.

Let $X\xrightarrow{i}Y\to Z$ be a fiber sequence of $k$ -fold loop spaces (where $k\geq 1$ ), and let $R$ be an $\mathbf{E}_{{m}}$ -ring for $m\geq k+1$ . Suppose that $\mu:Y\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)$ is a map of $k$ -fold loop spaces. Then, there is a $k$ -fold loop map $\phi:Z\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(X^{\mu\circ i})$ whose Thom spectrum is equivalent to $Y^{\mu}$ as $\mathbf{E}_{{k-1}}$ -rings. Concisely, if arrows are labeled by their associated Thom spectra, then there is a diagram

### 2.2. The Hopkins-Mahowald theorem

The primary motivation for this project is the following miracle (see [Mah79] for $p=2$ and [MRS01, Lemma 3.3] for $p>2$ , as well as [AB19, Theorem 5.1] for a proof of the equivalence as one of $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -algebras):

#### Theorem 2.2.1 (Hopkins-Mahowald).

Let $\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p}$ be the $p$ -completion of the sphere at a prime $p$ , and let $f:S^{1}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p})$ detect the element $1-p\in\pi_{1}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p})\simeq\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}$ . Let $\mu:\Omega^{2}S^{3}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p})$ denote the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -map extending $f$ ; then there is a $p$ -complete equivalence $(\Omega^{2}S^{3})^{\mu}\to\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ of $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring spectra.

It is not too hard to deduce the following result from Theorem 2.2.1:

#### Corollary 2.2.2.

Let $S^{3}\langle 3\rangle$ denote the $3$ -connected cover of $S^{3}$ . Then the Thom spectrum of the composite $\Omega^{2}S^{3}\langle 3\rangle\to\Omega^{2}S^{3}\xrightarrow{\mu}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p})$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ as an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring.

#### Remark 2.2.3.

Theorem 2.2.1 implies a restrictive version of the nilpotence theorem: if $R$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring spectrum, and $x\in\pi_{\ast}R$ is a simple $p$ -torsion element which has trivial $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -Hurewicz image, then $x$ is nilpotent. This is explained in [MNN15, Proposition 4.19]. Indeed, to show that $x$ is nilpotent, it suffices to show that the localization $R[1/x]$ is contractible. Since $px=0$ , the localization $R[1/x]$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring in which $p=0$ , so the universal property of Theorem 2.1.7 implies that there is an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -map $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}\to R[1/x]$ . It follows that the unit $R\to R[1/x]$ factors through the Hurewicz map $R\to R\wedge\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ . In particular, the multiplication by $x$ map on $R[1/x]$ factors as the indicated dotted map:

$$ \textstyle{\Sigma^{|x|}R\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{x} \textstyle{R\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{R[1/x].} \textstyle{\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}\wedge\Sigma^{|x|}R\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{x} \textstyle{R\wedge\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} $$

However, the bottom map is null (because $x$ has trivial $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -Hurewicz image), so $x$ must be null in $\pi_{\ast}R[1/x]$ . This is possible if and only if $R[1/x]$ is contractible, as desired. See Proposition 5.4.1 for the analogous connection between Corollary 2.2.2 and nilpotence.

Since an argument similar to the proof of Theorem 2.2.1 will be necessary later in Step 2 of Section 5.2, we will recall a proof of this theorem. The key non-formal input is the following result of Steinberger’s from [BMMS86, Theorems III.2.2 and III.2.3]:

#### Theorem 2.2.4 (Steinberger).

Let $\zeta_{i}$ denote the conjugate to the Milnor generators $\xi_{i}$ of the dual Steenrod algebra, and similarly for $\tau_{i}$ at odd primes. Then

$$ Q^{p^{i}}\zeta_{i}=\zeta_{i+1},\ Q^{p^{j}}\tau_{j}=\tau_{j+1} $$

for $i,j+1>0$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 2.2.1.

By Corollary 2.1.7, the Thom spectrum $(\Omega^{2}S^{3})^{\mu}$ is the free $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring with a nullhomotopy of $p$ . Since $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring with a nullhomotopy of $p$ , we obtain an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -map $(\Omega^{2}S^{3})^{\mu}\to\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ . To prove that this map is a $p$ -complete equivalence, it suffices to prove that it induces an isomorphism on mod $p$ homology.

The mod $p$ homology of $(\Omega^{2}S^{3})^{\mu}$ can be calculated directly via the Thom isomorphism $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}\wedge(\Omega^{2}S^{3})^{\mu}\simeq\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}\wedge\Sigma^{\infty}_{+}\Omega^{2}S^{3}$ . Note that this is not an equivalence as $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}\wedge\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -comodules: the Thom twisting is highly nontrivial.

For simplicity, we will now specialize to the case $p=2$ , although the same proof works at odd primes. The homology of $\Omega^{2}S^{3}$ is classical: it is a polynomial ring generated by applying $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -Dyer-Lashof operations to a single generator $x_{1}$ in degree $1$ . Theorem 2.2.4 implies that the same is true for the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra: it, too, is a polynomial ring generated by applying $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -Dyer-Lashof operations to the single generator $\zeta_{1}=\xi_{1}$ in degree $1$ . Since the map $(\Omega^{2}S^{3})^{\mu}\to\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{2}$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring map, it preserves $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -Dyer-Lashof operations on mod $p$ homology. By the above discussion, it suffices to show that the generator $x_{1}\in\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega^{2}S^{3})^{\mu}\cong\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega^{2}S^{3})$ in degree $1$ is mapped to $\zeta_{1}\in\mathrm{H}_{\ast}\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{2}$ .

To prove this, note that $x_{1}$ is the image of the generator in degree $1$ in homology under the double suspension $S^{1}\to\Omega^{2}S^{3}$ , and that $\zeta_{1}$ is the image of the generator in degree $1$ in homology under the canonical map $\mathbb{S}/p\to\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ . It therefore suffices to show that the Thom spectrum of the spherical fibration $S^{1}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p})$ detecting $1-p$ is simply $\mathbb{S}/p$ . This is an easy exercise. ∎

#### Remark 2.2.5.

When $p=2$ , one does not need to $p$ -complete in Theorem 2.2.1: the map $S^{1}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{2})$ factors as $S^{1}\to\mathrm{BO}\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ , where the first map detects the Möbius bundle over $S^{1}$ , and the second map is the $J$ -homomorphism.

#### Notation 2.2.6.

Let $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ denote the (operadic nerve of the) cup-1 operad from [Law20, Example 1.3.6]: this is the operad whose $n$ th space is empty unless $n=2$ , in which case it is $S^{1}$ with the antipodal action of $\Sigma_{2}$ . We will need to slightly modify the definition of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ when localized at an odd prime $p$ : in this case, it will denote the operad whose $n$ th space is a point if $n<p$ , empty if $n>p$ , and when $n=p$ is the ordered configuration space $\mathrm{Conf}_{p}(\mathbf{R}^{2})$ with the permutation action of $\Sigma_{p}$ . Any homotopy commutative ring admits the structure of a $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -algebra at $p=2$ , but at other primes it is slightly stronger to be a $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -algebra than to be a homotopy commutative ring. If $k\geq 2$ , any $\mathbf{E}_{{k}}$ -algebra structure on a spectrum restricts to a $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -algebra structure.

#### Remark 2.2.7.

As stated in [Law20, Proposition 1.5.29], the operation $Q_{1}$ already exists in the mod $2$ homology of any $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -ring $R$ , where $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ is the cup-1 operad from Notation 2.2.6 — the entire $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -structure is not necessary. With our modification of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ at odd primes as in Remark 2.2.6, this is also true at odd primes.

#### Remark 2.2.8.

We will again momentarily specialize to $p=2$ for convenience. Steinberger’s calculation in Theorem 2.2.4 can be rephrased as stating that $Q_{1}\zeta_{i}=\zeta_{i+1}$ , where $Q_{1}$ is the lower-indexed Dyer-Lashof operation. (See [BMMS86, Page 59] for this notation.) As in Remark 2.2.7, the operation $Q_{1}$ already exists in the mod $p$ homology of any $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -ring $R$ . The argument with Dyer-Lashof operations and Theorem 2.2.4 used in the proof of Theorem 2.2.1 will be referred to as the Dyer-Lashof hopping argument. It will be used again (in the same manner) in the proof of Theorem A.

Theorem 2.2.1 is equivalent to Steinberger’s calculation (Theorem 2.2.4), as well as to Bökstedt’s calculation of $\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ (as a ring spectrum, and not just the calculation of its homotopy). ### 2.3. No-go theorems for higher chromatic heights

In light of Theorem 2.2.1 and Corollary 2.2.2, it is natural to wonder if appropriate higher chromatic analogues of $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ and $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{Z}$ , such as $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle$ , $\mathrm{bo}$ , or $\mathrm{tmf}$ can be realized as Thom spectra of spherical fibrations. The answer is known to be negative (see [Mah87, Rud98, Cha19]) in many cases:

#### Theorem 2.3.1 (Mahowald, Rudyak, Chatham).

There is no space $X$ with a spherical fibration $\mu:X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ (even after completion) such that $X^{\mu}$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{BP}\langle{1}\rangle$ or $\mathrm{bo}$ . Moreover, there is no $2$ -local loop space $X^{\prime}$ with a spherical fibration determined by an H-map $\mu:X^{\prime}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{2})$ such that ${X^{\prime}}^{\mu}$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{tmf}^{\wedge}_{2}$ .

The proofs rely on calculations in the unstable homotopy groups of spheres.

#### Remark 2.3.2.

Although not written down anywhere, a slight modification of the argument used by Mahowald to show that $\mathrm{bu}$ is not the Thom spectrum of a spherical fibration over a loop space classified by an H-map can be used to show that $\mathrm{BP}\langle{2}\rangle$ at $p=2$ (i.e., $\mathrm{tmf}_{1}(3)$ ) is not the Thom spectrum of a spherical fibration over a loop space classified by an H-map. We do not know a proof that $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle$ is not the Thom spectrum of a spherical fibration over a loop space classified by an H-map for all $n\geq 1$ and all primes, but we strongly suspect this to be true.

#### Remark 2.3.3.

A lesser-known no-go result due to Priddy appears in [Lew78, Chapter 2.11], where it is shown that $\mathrm{BP}$ cannot appear as the Thom spectrum of a double loop map $\Omega^{2}X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ . In fact, the argument shows that the same result is true with $\mathrm{BP}$ replaced by $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle$ for $n\geq 1$ ; we had independently come up with this argument for $\mathrm{BP}\langle{1}\rangle$ before learning about Priddy’s argument. Since Lewis’ thesis is not particularly easy to acquire, we give a sketch of Priddy’s argument. By the Thom isomorphism and the calculation (see [LN14, Theorem 4.3], as well as [Wil75, Proposition 1.7] and [AR05, Proposition 5.3]):

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle;\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\begin{cases}\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1}^{2},\cdots,\zeta_{n-1}^{2},\zeta_{n}^{2},\zeta_{n+1},\cdots]&p=2,\\
\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\cdots]\otimes\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}_{p}}(\tau_{n},\tau_{n+1},\cdots)&p>2,\end{cases} $$

we find that the mod $p$ homology of $\Omega^{2}X$ would be isomorphic as an algebra to a polynomial ring on infinitely many generators, possibly tensored with an exterior algebra on infinitely many generators. The Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequence then implies that the mod $p$ cohomology of $X$ is given by

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\begin{cases}\mathbf{F}_{2}[b_{1},\cdots,b_{n},c_{n+1},\cdots]&p=2,\\
\mathbf{F}_{p}[b_{1},b_{2},\cdots]\otimes\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}_{p}}(c_{n+1},\cdots)&p>2,\end{cases} $$

where $|b_{i}|=2p^{i}$ and $|c_{i}|=2p^{i-1}+1$ . If $p$ is odd, then since $|b_{1}|=2p$ , we have $\mathrm{P}^{p}(b_{1})=b_{1}^{p}$ . Liulevicius’ formula for $\mathrm{P}^{1}$ in terms of secondary cohomology operations ([Liu62, Theorem 1]) allows us to write $\mathrm{P}^{p}(b_{1})$ as a sum $c_{0}\mathcal{R}(b_{1})+\sum_{\gamma}c_{0,\gamma}\Gamma_{\gamma}(b_{1})$ , where $\mathcal{R}(b_{1})$ is a coset in $\mathrm{H}^{2p+4(p-1)}(X;\mathbf{F}_{p})$ and $\Gamma_{\gamma}$ is an operation of odd degree, so that $\Gamma_{\gamma}(b_{1})$ is in odd degree. We will not need to know what exactly the sum is indexed by, or what any of these operations are. Observe that $\Gamma_{\gamma}$ kills $b_{1}$ because everything is concentrated in even degrees in the relevant range, and $\mathcal{R}$ also kills $b_{1}$ since $|\mathcal{R}(b_{1})|=4(p-1)+2p^{i}$ is never a sum of numbers of the form $2p^{k}$ when $p>2$ . Using this, one can conclude that $b_{1}^{p}=0$ , which is a contradiction. A similar calculation works at $p=2$ , using Adams’ study of secondary mod $2$ cohomology operations in [Ada60].

#### Remark 2.3.4.

Using the calculations of $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{bo})$ and $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{ku})$ from [AHL10], Angeltveit-Hill-Lawson show in [AHL09] that neither $\mathrm{bo}$ not $\mathrm{ku}$ can appear as the Thom spectrum of a double loop map $\Omega^{2}X\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ .

### 3.1. Ravenel’s $X(n)$ spectra

The proof of the nilpotence theorem in [DHS88, HS98] crucially relied upon certain Thom spectra arising from Bott periodicity; these spectra first appeared in Ravenel’s seminal paper [Rav84].

#### Definition 3.1.1.

Let $X(n)$ denote the Thom spectrum of the $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -map $\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)\subseteq\mathrm{BU}\xrightarrow{J}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ , where the first map arises from Bott periodicity.

#### Example 3.1.2.

The $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -ring $X(1)$ is the sphere spectrum, while $X(\infty)$ is $\mathrm{MU}$ . Since the map $\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)\to\mathrm{BU}$ is an equivalence in dimensions $\leq 2n-2$ , the same is true for the map $X(n)\to\mathrm{MU}$ ; the first dimension in which $X(n)$ has an element in its homotopy which is not detected by $\mathrm{MU}$ is $2n-1$ .

#### Remark 3.1.3.

The $\mathbf{E}_{{2}}$ -structure on $X(n)$ does not extend to an $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -structure (see [Law20, Example 1.5.31]). If $X(n)$ admits such an $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -structure, then the induced map $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(X(n))\to\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p})$ on mod $p$ homology would commute with $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -Dyer-Lashof operations. However, we know that the image of $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(X(n))$ in $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p})$ is $\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1}^{2},\cdots,\zeta_{n}^{2}]$ ; since Steinberger’s calculation (Theorem 2.2.4) implies that $Q_{2}(\zeta_{i}^{2})=\zeta_{i+1}^{2}$ via the relation $Q_{2}(x^{2})=Q_{1}(x)^{2}$ , we find that the image of $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(X(n))$ in $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p})$ cannot be closed under the $\mathbf{E}_{{3}}$ -Dyer-Lashof operation $Q_{2}$ .

#### Remark 3.1.4.

The proof of the nilpotence theorem shows that each of the $X(n)$ detects nilpotence. However, it is known (see [Rav84, Theorem 3.1]) that $\langle X(n)\rangle>\langle X(n+1)\rangle$ .

After localizing at a prime $p$ , the spectrum $\mathrm{MU}$ splits as a wedge of suspensions of $\mathrm{BP}$ ; this splitting comes from the Quillen idempotent on $\mathrm{MU}$ . The same is true of the $X(n)$ spectra, as explained in [Rav86, Section 6.5]: a multiplicative map $X(n)_{(p)}\to X(n)_{(p)}$ is determined by a polynomial $f(x)=\sum_{0\leq i\leq n-1}a_{i}x^{i+1}$ , with $a_{0}=1$ and $a_{i}\in\pi_{2i}(X(n)_{(p)})$ . One can use this to define a truncated form of the Quillen idempotent $\epsilon_{n}$ on $X(n)_{(p)}$ (see [Hop84, Proposition 1.3.7]), and thereby obtain a summand of $X(n)_{(p)}$ . We summarize the necessary results in the following theorem.

#### Theorem 3.1.5.

Let $n$ be such that $p^{n}\leq k\leq p^{n+1}-1$ . Then $X(k)_{(p)}$ splits as a wedge of suspensions of the spectrum $T(n)=\epsilon_{p^{n}}\cdot X(p^{n})_{(p)}$ .

- • The map $T(n)\to\mathrm{BP}$ is an equivalence in dimensions $\leq|v_{n+1}|-2$ , so there is an indecomposable element $v_{i}\in\pi_{\ast}T(n)$ which maps to an indecomposable element in $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{BP}$ for $0\leq i\leq n$ .

- • This map induces the inclusion $\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}T(n)=\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}[t_{1},\cdots,t_{n}]\subseteq\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(\mathrm{BP})$ on $\mathrm{BP}$ -homology, and the inclusions $\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1}^{2},\cdots,\zeta_{n}^{2}]\subseteq\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1}^{2},\zeta_{2}^{2},\cdots]$ and $\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1},\cdots,\zeta_{n}]\subseteq\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\cdots]$ on mod $2$ and mod $p$ homology.

It is known that that $T(n)$ admits the structure of an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring (see [BL21, Section 7.5]). $$ \mathrm{B}\mathrm{Sp}(2)\to\mathrm{BSU}(4)\to\mathrm{BSU}\simeq\mathrm{B}^{3}\mathrm{U}. $$

The map $\mu$ admits a description as the left vertical map in the following map of fiber sequences:

$$ \textstyle{\Omega V_{2}(\mathbf{H}^{2})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mu} \textstyle{\Omega S^{7}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{S^{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{BU}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\ast\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{B}^{2}\mathrm{U}.} $$

It is possible to construct $X(n+1)$ as an $X(n)$ -algebra (see also [Bea18]):

#### Construction 3.1.10.

There is a fiber sequence

$$ \Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)\to\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n+1)\to\Omega S^{2n+1}. $$

$$ \Omega^{2}S^{2n+1}\to\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)\to\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n+1)\to\Omega\mathrm{SU}\simeq\mathrm{BU}, $$

where the first two maps form a fiber sequence. By Proposition 2.1.6, $X(n+1)$ is the free $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ - $X(n)$ -algebra with a nullhomotopy of $\chi_{n}$ .

#### Remark 3.1.11.

Another construction of the map $\chi_{n}\in\pi_{2n-1}X(n)$ from Construction 3.1.10 is as follows. $$ S^{2n-1}\to\Sigma^{-2}\mathbf{C}P^{n}\to X(n), $$

where the top row is a cofiber sequence, and the bottom row is a fiber sequence.

### 3.2. Related Thom spectra

We now introduce several Thom spectra related to the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -rings $T(n)$ described in the previous section; some of these were introduced in [Dev19b]. (Relationships to $T(n)$ will be further discussed in Section 6.2.) For the reader’s convenience, we have included a table of the spectra introduced below with internal references to their definitions at the beginning of this section.

#### Remark 3.2.1.

Recall (e.g., from [Rav86, Section 4.4]) that under the map

$$ \mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(\mathrm{BP})\cong\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}[t_{1},t_{2},\cdots]\to\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{BP};\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\begin{cases}\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1}^{2},\zeta_{2}^{2},\cdots]&p=2,\\
\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\cdots]&p>2,\end{cases} $$

the class $t_{i}$ is sent to $\zeta_{i}^{2}$ (resp. $\zeta_{i}$ ) modulo decomposables when $p=2$ (resp. $p>2$ ). Moreover, under the map

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{BP};\mathbf{F}_{p})\to\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p};\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\begin{cases}\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\cdots]&p=2,\\
\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\cdots]\otimes E(\tau_{0},\tau_{1},\cdots)&p>2,\end{cases} $$

the classes $\zeta_{i+1}$ (resp. $\tau_{i}$ ) at $p=2$ (resp. $p>2$ ) detect a nullhomotopy of $v_{i}\in\pi_{2p^{i}-2}\mathrm{BP}$ in $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}\otimes\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ . This implies, for instance, that if $X$ is a spectrum such that $\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(X)\simeq\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}/(p,\cdots,v_{j-1})[t_{1},\cdots,t_{m}]$ with $j\leq m$ , then $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(X;\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1},\cdots,\zeta_{m}]\otimes E(\tau_{1},\cdots,\tau_{j-1})$ for $p>2$ , and $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(X;\mathbf{F}_{2})\cong\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1}^{2},\cdots,\zeta_{j}^{2},\zeta_{j+1},\cdots,\zeta_{m}]$ .

The following Thom spectrum was introduced in [MRS01].

#### Definition 3.2.2.

Let $y(n)$ denote the Thom spectrum of the composite

$$ \Omega J_{p^{n}-1}(S^{2})\to\Omega^{2}S^{3}\xrightarrow{1-p}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p}). $$

If $J_{p^{n}-1}(S^{2})\langle 2\rangle$ denotes the $2$ -connected cover of $J_{p^{n}-1}(S^{2})$ , then let $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ denote the Thom spectrum of the composite

$$ \Omega J_{p^{n}-1}(S^{2})\langle 2\rangle\to\Omega^{2}S^{3}\langle 3\rangle\to\Omega^{2}S^{3}\xrightarrow{1-p}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{\wedge}_{p}), $$

so that both $y(n)$ and $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ admit the structure of $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -rings via [AB19, Corollary 3.2].

#### Proposition 3.2.3.

As $\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}\mathrm{BP}$ -comodules, we have

$$ \mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(y(n))\cong\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}/I_{n}[t_{1},\cdots,t_{n}],\ \mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n))\cong\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}/(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n-1})[t_{1},\cdots,t_{n}], $$

where $I_{n}$ denotes the invariant ideal $(p,v_{1},\cdots,v_{n-1})$ .

#### Proof.

The claim for $y(n)$ is [MRS01, Equation 2.8]. There is an equivalence $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)/p\simeq y(n)$ , so that $\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n))/p\simeq\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(y(n))$ . The Bockstein spectral sequence collapses, and the extensions on the $E_{\infty}$ -page simply place $p$ in filtration $1$ . This implies the second equivalence. ∎

One corollary is the following; this can be deduced from Proposition 3.2.3 using Remark 3.2.1. We also refer to [AQ19, Lemma 2.3] for a direct proof of the following.

#### Corollary 3.2.4.

As $A_{\ast}$ -comodules, we have

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\ast}(y(n);\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\begin{cases}\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\cdots,\zeta_{n}]&p=2\\
\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\cdots,\zeta_{n}]\otimes E(\tau_{0},\cdots,\tau_{n-1})&p\geq 3,\end{cases} $$

and

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\ast}(y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n);\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\begin{cases}\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1}^{2},\zeta_{2},\cdots,\zeta_{n}]&p=2\\
\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\cdots,\zeta_{n}]\otimes E(\tau_{1},\cdots,\tau_{n-1})&p\geq 3.\end{cases} $$

We will now relate $y(n)$ and $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ to $T(n)$ .

#### Construction 3.2.5.

Let $m\leq n$ , and let $I_{m}$ be the ideal generated by $p,v_{1},\cdots,v_{m-1}$ , where the $v_{i}$ are some choices of indecomposables in $\pi_{|v_{i}|}(T(n))$ which form a regular sequence. Inductively define $T(n)/I_{m}$ as the cofiber of the map

$$ T(n)/I_{m-1}\xrightarrow{v_{m}\wedge 1}T(n)\wedge T(n)/I_{m-1}\to T(n)/I_{m-1}. $$

The $\mathrm{BP}$ -homology of $T(n)/I_{m}$ is $\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}/I_{m}[t_{1},\cdots,t_{n}]$ . The spectrum $T(n)/(v_{1},\cdots,v_{m-1})$ is defined similarly.

#### Proposition 3.2.6.

Let $p>2$ . There is an equivalence between $T(n)/I_{n}$ (resp. $T(n)/(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n-1})$ ) and the spectrum $y(n)$ (resp. $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ ) of Definition 3.2.2.

#### Proof.

We will prove the result for $y(n)$ ; the analogous proof works for $y_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)$ . By [Gra89a], the space $\Omega J_{p^{n}-1}(S^{2})$ is homotopy commutative (since $p>2$ ). Moreover, the map $\Omega J_{p^{n}-1}(S^{2})\to\Omega^{2}S^{3}$ is an H-map, so $y(n)$ is a homotopy commutative $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring spectrum. It is known (see [Rav86, Section 6.5]) that homotopy commutative maps $T(n)\to y(n)$ are equivalent to partial complex orientations of $y(n)$ , i.e., factorizations

$$ \textstyle{\mathbb{S}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{1} \textstyle{\Sigma^{-2}\mathbf{C}P^{p^{n}-1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\gamma_{n}} \textstyle{y(n).} $$

Such a $\gamma_{n}$ indeed exists by obstruction theory: suppose $k<p^{n}-1$ , and we have a map $\Sigma^{-2}\mathbf{C}P^{k}\to y(n)$ . Since there is a cofiber sequence

$$ S^{2k-1}\to\Sigma^{-2}\mathbf{C}P^{k}\to\Sigma^{-2}\mathbf{C}P^{k+1} $$

of spectra, the obstruction to extending along $\Sigma^{-2}\mathbf{C}P^{k+1}$ is an element of $\pi_{2k-1}y(n)$ . However, the homotopy of $y(n)$ is concentrated in even degrees in the appropriate range, so a choice of $\gamma_{n}$ does indeed exist. Moreover, this choice can be made such that they fit into a compatible family in the sense that there is a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{\Sigma^{-2}\mathbf{C}P^{p^{n}-1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\gamma_{n}} \textstyle{\Sigma^{-2}\mathbf{C}P^{p^{n+1}-1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\gamma_{n+1}} \textstyle{y(n)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{y(n+1).} $$

The formal group law over $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ has infinite height; this forces the elements $p,v_{1},\cdots,v_{n-1}$ (defined for the “ $(p^{n}-1)$ -bud” on $\pi_{\ast}y(n)$ ) to vanish in the homotopy of $y(n)$ . It follows that the orientation $T(n)\to y(n)$ constructed above factors through the quotient $T(n)/I_{n}$ . The induced map $T(n)/I_{n}\to y(n)$ can be seen to be an isomorphism on homology (via, for instance, Definition 3.2.2 and Construction 3.2.5). ∎

#### Remark 3.2.7.

Since $y(n)$ has a $v_{n}$ -self-map, we can form the spectrum $y(n)/v_{n}$ ; its mod $p$ homology is

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\ast}(y(n)/v_{n};\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\begin{cases}\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1},\cdots,\zeta_{n}]\otimes\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}_{2}}(\zeta_{n+1})&p=2\\
\mathbf{F}_{p}[\zeta_{1},\cdots,\zeta_{n}]\otimes\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}_{p}}(\tau_{0},\cdots,\tau_{n-1},\tau_{n})&p\geq 3.\end{cases} $$

#### Definition 3.2.8.

Let $S^{4}\to\mathrm{BSpin}$ denote the generator of $\pi_{4}\mathrm{BSpin}\cong\mathbf{Z}$ , and let $\Omega S^{5}\to\mathrm{BSpin}$ denote the extension of this map, which classifies a real vector bundle of virtual dimension zero over $\Omega S^{5}$ . #### Remark 3.2.9.

As mentioned in the introduction, the spectrum $A$ has been intensely studied by Mahowald and his coauthors in (for instance) [Mah79, DM81, Mah81b, Mah81a, Mah82, MU77], where it is often denoted $X_{5}$ .

#### Remark 3.2.10.

The map $\Omega S^{5}\to\mathrm{BSpin}$ is one of $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -spaces, so the Thom spectrum $A$ admits the structure of an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring with an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -map $A\to\mathrm{MSpin}$ .

#### Remark 3.2.11.

There are multiple equivalent ways to characterize this Thom spectrum. Note that $A$ is defined integrally, and not just $p$ -locally for some prime $p$ .

There is a canonical map $A\to T(1)$ of $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -rings, constructed as follows. By the universal property of $A$ , it suffices to prove that the unit $\mathbb{S}\to T(1)$ extends along the inclusion $\mathbb{S}\to C\nu$ , i.e., that $\nu=0\in\pi_{3}T(1)$ up to units. #### Theorem 3.3.1 ([Lur16, Example 5.5.4.16], [Fra13, Definition 2.5]).

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a symmetric monoidal presentable $\infty$ -category, and let $A$ be an $\mathbf{E}_{{k}}$ -algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ . #### Example 3.3.11.

The element $\chi_{2}\in\pi_{3}X(2)$ is central. It therefore suffices to show that $\chi_{2}$ is central after $p$ -localizing for all $p$ . First, note that $\chi_{2}$ is torsion, so it is nullhomotopic (and therefore central) after rationalization. Next, if $p>2$ , then $X(2)_{(p)}$ splits as a wedge of suspensions of spheres. ## 4. Review of some unstable homotopy theory

### 4.1. Charming and Gray maps

A major milestone in unstable homotopy theory was Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer’s result on the $p$ -exponent of unstable homotopy groups of spheres from [CMN79a, CMN79b, Nei81]. They defined for all $p>2$ and $k\geq 1$ a map $\phi_{n}:\Omega^{2}S^{2n+1}\to S^{2n-1}$ (the integer $k$ is assumed implicit) such that the composite of $\phi_{n}$ with the double suspension $E^{2}:S^{2n-1}\to\Omega^{2}S^{2n+1}$ is homotopic to the $p^{k}$ -th power map. By induction on $n$ , they concluded via a result of Selick’s (see [Sel77]) that $p^{n}$ kills the $p$ -primary component of the homotopy of $S^{2n+1}$ . Such maps will be important in the rest of this article, so we will isolate their desired properties in the definition of a charming map, inspired by [ST19]. (Our choice of terminology is non-standard, and admittedly horrible, but it does not seem like the literature has chosen any naming convention for the sort of maps we desire.)

#### Definition 4.1.1.

A $p$ -local map $f:\Omega^{2}S^{2np+1}\to S^{2np-1}$ is called a Gray map if the composite of $f$ with the double suspension $E^{2}$ is the degree $p$ map, and the composite

$$ \Omega^{2}S^{2n+1}\xrightarrow{\Omega H}\Omega^{2}S^{2np+1}\xrightarrow{f}S^{2np-1} $$

is nullhomotopic. Moreover, a $p$ -local map $f:\Omega^{2}S^{2np+1}\to S^{2np-1}$ is called a charming map if the composite of $f$ with the double suspension $E^{2}$ is the degree $p$ map, the fiber of $f$ admits the structure of a $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -space, and if there is a space $BK$ which sits in a fiber sequence

$$ S^{2np-1}\to BK\to\Omega S^{2np+1} $$

such that the boundary map $\Omega^{2}S^{2np+1}\to S^{2np-1}$ is homotopic to $f$ .

#### Remark 4.1.2.

If $f$ is a charming map, then the fiber of $f$ is a loop space. Indeed, $\fib(f)\simeq\Omega BK$ .

#### Example 4.1.3.

Let $f$ denote the Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer map with $k=1$ . Anick proved (see [Ani93, GT10]) that the fiber of $f$ admits a delooping, i.e., there is a space $T^{2np+1}(p)$ (now known as an Anick space) which sits in a fiber sequence

$$ S^{2np-1}\to T^{2np+1}(p)\to\Omega S^{2np+1}. $$

It follows that $f$ is a charming map.

#### Remark 4.1.4.

We claim that $T^{2p+1}(p)=\Omega S^{3}\langle 3\rangle$ , where $S^{3}\langle 3\rangle$ is the $3$ -connected cover of $S^{3}$ . To prove this, we will construct a $p$ -local fiber sequence

$$ S^{2p-1}\to\Omega S^{3}\langle 3\rangle\to\Omega S^{2p+1}. $$

This fiber sequence was originally constructed by Toda in [Tod62]. To construct this fiber sequence, we first note that there is a $p$ -local fiber sequence

$$ S^{2p-1}\to J_{p-1}(S^{2})\to\mathbf{C}P^{\infty}, $$

where the first map is the factorization of $\alpha_{1}:S^{2p-1}\to\Omega S^{3}$ through the $2(p-1)$ -skeleton of $\Omega S^{3}$ , and the second map is the composite $J_{p-1}(S^{2})\to\Omega S^{3}\to\mathbf{C}P^{\infty}$ . This fiber sequence is simply an odd-primary version of the Hopf fibration $S^{3}\to S^{2}\to\mathbf{C}P^{\infty}$ ; the identification of the fiber of the map $J_{p-1}(S^{2})\to\mathbf{C}P^{\infty}$ is a simple exercise with the Serre spectral sequence. Next, we have the EHP sequence

$$ J_{p-1}(S^{2})\to\Omega S^{3}\to\Omega S^{2p+1}. $$

Since $\Omega S^{3}\langle 3\rangle$ is the fiber of the map $\Omega S^{3}\to\mathbf{C}P^{\infty}$ , the desired fiber sequence is obtained by taking vertical fibers in the following map of fiber sequences:

$$ \textstyle{J_{p-1}(S^{2})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Omega S^{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Omega S^{2p+1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{C}P^{\infty}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{C}P^{\infty}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\ast.} $$

#### Example 4.1.5.

Let $W_{n}$ denote the fiber of the double suspension $S^{2n-1}\to\Omega^{2}S^{2n+1}$ . Gray proved in [Gra89b, Gra88] that $W_{n}$ admits a delooping $BW_{n}$ , and that after $p$ -localization, there is a fiber sequence

$$ BW_{n}\to\Omega^{2}S^{2np+1}\xrightarrow{f}S^{2np-1} $$

for some map $f$ . As suggested by the naming convention, $f$ is a Gray map.

As proved in [ST19], Gray maps satisfy an important rigidity property:

#### Proposition 4.1.6 (Selick-Theriault).

The fiber of any Gray map admits an H-space structure, and is H-equivalent to $BW_{n}$ .

#### Remark 4.1.7.

It has been conjectured by Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer and Gray in the papers cited above that there is an equivalence $BW_{n}\simeq\Omega T^{2np+1}(p)$ , and that $\Omega T^{2np+1}(p)$ retracts off of $\Omega^{2}P^{2np+1}(p)$ as an H-space, where $P^{k}(p)$ is the mod $p$ Moore space $S^{k-1}\cup_{p}e^{k}$ with top cell in dimension $k$ . For our purposes, we shall require something slightly stronger: namely, the retraction should be one of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -spaces. The first part of this conjecture would follow from Proposition 4.1.6 if the Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer map were a Gray map. In [Ame20], it is shown that the existence of $p$ -primary elements of Kervaire invariant one would imply equivalences of the form $BW_{p^{n-1}}\simeq\Omega T^{2p^{n}+1}(p)$ .

Motivated by Remark 4.1.7 and Proposition 4.1.6, we state the following conjecture; it is slightly weaker than the conjecture mentioned in Remark 4.1.7, and is an amalgamation of slight modifications of conjectures of Cohen, Moore, Neisendorfer, Gray, and Mahowald in unstable homotopy theory, as well as an analogue of Proposition 4.1.6. (For instance, we strengthen having an H-space retraction to having a $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ -space retraction).

#### Conjecture D.

The following statements are true:

- (a) The homotopy fiber of any charming map is equivalent as a loop space to the loop space on an Anick space.

### 5.1. Statement of the theorem

To state the main theorem of this section, we set some notation. Fix an integer $n\geq 1$ , and work in the $p$ -complete stable category. For each Thom spectrum $R$ of height $n-1$ in Table 1, let $\sigma_{n-1}:S^{|\sigma_{n-1}|}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)$ denote a map detecting $\sigma_{n-1}\in\pi_{|\sigma_{n-1}|}(R)$ (which exists by Theorem 3.2.25). #### Theorem A.

Let $R$ be a height $n-1$ spectrum as in the second line of Table 1. #### Proof of Theorem C.

First, note that such a splitting exists after rationalization. Indeed, it suffices to check that this is true on rational homotopy; since the orientations under considerations are ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring maps, the induced map on homotopy is one of rings. We now show that the generators of $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{tmf}\otimes\mathbf{Q}\cong\mathbf{Q}[c_{4},c_{6}]$ lift to $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{MString}\otimes\mathbf{Q}$ . Although one can argue this by explicitly constructing manifold representatives (as is done for $c_{4}$ in [Dev19b, Corollary 6.3]), it is also possible to provide a more homotopy-theoretic proof: the elements $c_{4}$ and $c_{6}$ live in dimensions $8$ and $12$ respectively, and the map $\mathrm{MString}\to\mathrm{tmf}$ is known to be an equivalence in dimensions $\leq 15$ by [Hil, Theorem 2.1]. ### 6.2. Wood equivalences

The Wood equivalence states that $\mathrm{bo}\wedge C\eta\simeq\mathrm{bu}$ . There are generalizations of this equivalence to $\mathrm{tmf}$ (see [Mat16]); for instance, there is a $2$ -local $8$ -cell complex $DA_{1}$ whose cohomology is isomorphic to the double of $A(1)$ as an $A(2)$ -module such that $\mathrm{tmf}_{(2)}\wedge DA_{1}\simeq\mathrm{tmf}_{1}(3)\simeq\mathrm{BP}\langle{2}\rangle$ . Similarly, if $X_{3}$ denotes the $3$ -local $3$ -cell complex $S^{0}\cup_{\alpha_{1}}e^{4}\cup_{2\alpha_{1}}e^{8}$ , then $\mathrm{tmf}_{(3)}\wedge X_{3}\simeq\mathrm{tmf}_{1}(2)\simeq\mathrm{BP}\langle{2}\rangle\vee\Sigma^{8}\mathrm{BP}\langle{2}\rangle$ . We will use the umbrella term “Wood equivalence” to refer to equivalences of this kind.

Our goal in this section is to revisit these Wood equivalences using the point of view stemming from Theorem A. In particular, we propose that these equivalences are suggested by the existence of certain EHP sequences; we will greatly expand on this in a forthcoming document. We find this to be a rather beautiful connection between stable and unstable homotopy theory.

The first Wood-style result was proved in Proposition 3.2.6. The next result, originally proved in [Mah79, Section 2.5] and [DM81, Theorem 3.7], is the simplest example of a Wood-style equivalence which is related to the existence of certain EHP sequences.
